title: Riverlight Verses
author: Anonymous
excerpt:
The river keeps no calendar of its own,
only the long unspooling of water over stone.
I have stood on this bank in every season
and called it the same river, though it never is.

In spring the current runs loud with melted snow,
carrying twigs and the pale husks of winter.
In summer it slows to a murmur beneath the willows,
warm enough that children wade in without flinching.

By autumn the water has darkened with fallen leaves,
and the light on its surface turns the color of rust.
Winter freezes only the shallows near the shore,
leaving a black channel where the current still moves.

I think of the people who stood here before me,
filling jars, watering animals, washing cloth,
none of them thinking of the river as a symbol,
only as the thing that had to be crossed or used.

Now I come here with no task at all,
only the habit of watching water move,
as if watching long enough might explain
why nothing in a life stays the same shape twice.

The fish do not care that I am watching.
The herons do not care that I am watching.
Even the stones underfoot, worn smooth by centuries,
seem indifferent to whoever happens to be standing here.

And yet I keep coming back to this bend in the river,
as though it owed me an answer,
as though enough mornings spent here
would add up to something like understanding.

Maybe that is what a river is for:
not to answer, but to keep moving
while you stand still and change anyway,
carried along by something you cannot see.

So I let the water do what it does,
and I do what I do, which is watch,
and call it, for lack of a better word,
peace, though it is closer to attention.

masterNotes.context: This fixture stands in for a 19th-century public-domain poem excerpted for length rather than for rights reasons — the full poem runs well past the 60-line threshold for shipping poems in full.
masterNotes.form: Free verse organized in quatrains, each stanza tied to a season, building toward a closing meditation on attention versus answers.
keyImages: The river's surface turning "the color of rust" in autumn, marking the passage of a year in a single image.
The closing distinction between "peace" and "attention" as two names for the same unresolved feeling.
whatToNotice: Notice how each stanza moves through a season without ever naming the speaker's own life directly.
discussionQuestions: Why might the speaker resist calling the river a symbol?
What does the poem gain by ending on a distinction between two words rather than a clear statement?
How does the seasonal structure shape your sense of time passing across the excerpt?
